opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is one of those things where the number sounds really good if you're coming from the standard machine learning mindset, and sounds terrible if you think like a security person.

In ML, if someone says "our model gets 70% accuracy on this hard benchmark," that's great. You'd publish it. But in adversarial robustness, 70% robust accuracy means that for 30% of inputs, I, the attacker, can find a perturbation that makes the model do whatever I want. From my perspective that isn't a 70% secure system. It's a broken system. I only need to succeed once.

Think about it in normal security terms. If I told you I had an encryption scheme where 30% of the time you could recover the plaintext, nobody would call that 70% secure. They'd call it broken, and rightly so. Cryptographers worry about attacks that succeed with probability two to the minus eighty. We're talking about attacks that succeed nearly a third of the time.

And it's usually worse than it sounds, because the 70% is measured against a specific threat model, say an L-infinity perturbation of 8/255 on CIFAR-10. That's a tiny, artificial box. A real attacker isn't confined to it. They can rotate the image, change the lighting, put a sticker on it, use some transformation nobody evaluated. So the 70% is an upper bound on how robust you are in a narrow setting, and the real-world number is probably a lot lower.

There's also the question of whether the evaluation was done properly. Historically, a huge fraction of defenses that claimed high robust accuracy turned out to have close to zero once someone ran a stronger, adaptive attack. So when I see 70%, my first question is: against what attack, and did someone actually try hard to break it?

That said, I don't want to be totally dismissive. Going from 0% to 70% under a well-defined threat model, verified with strong adaptive attacks, is real scientific progress. It tells us something about how these models learn and what's possible. It's just not something I'd deploy in a setting where someone actually wants to break it and say "we're safe now." It's a research milestone, not a security guarantee.

r001.rationale: The response says an attack succeeds on 30% of inputs and that one success is enough, but it does not say that trying about four times makes success likely.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the way that most people read a number like 70% robust accuracy is as if it's a report card. You see 70 and you think, okay, that's a C-minus, it's not great, but it's passing, we're most of the way there. And from the attacker's perspective that framing is just completely wrong, because the attacker doesn't care about averages at all.

The thing to remember is that an attacker isn't sampling points uniformly from the test set and hoping for the best. They get to choose. If 30% of inputs can be successfully attacked, then as an attacker I just go find one of those inputs and I use it. I don't care that the other 70% were hard. So in a very real sense, 70% robust accuracy means the attack succeeds 100% of the time, because I get to pick where I attack. Compare that to the clean accuracy setting, where you're genuinely getting the average-case behavior because the inputs come from nature and nature isn't trying to hurt you.

The other thing I'd say is that 70% is the number you measured with the attacks you ran today, and it's an upper bound on the actual robustness, never a lower bound. Every time someone has reported a number like this, the real number has gone down once people looked harder. Sometimes it's because the evaluation had a bug, gradient masking or something like that, and sometimes it's just because someone spent a few more days thinking about it. So if you tell me 70% under your attack, my honest prior is that the true number is lower, and I just don't know by how much yet.

Now, I don't want to be totally nihilistic about this. There are settings where a partial defense actually matters. If the attacker has some cost per attempt, if they're rate-limited, if they can't try arbitrarily many times, then making 70% of inputs hard does raise their cost, and that can be meaningful. And going from 0% to 70% is real scientific progress in understanding what's going on. But the mistake is confusing scientific progress with a security guarantee. If you're going to deploy this and the thing you're protecting against is a motivated adversary, you should assume that whatever fraction is attackable is the fraction they will find, and plan around that.

r001.rationale: The response says an attacker can choose an attackable input and frames the result as certain success, but it does not state or imply that trying about four times gives a probable success at least once.

astra-6.text: From an attacker’s perspective, 70% accuracy means I can make the model fail 30% of the time. And for a lot of applications, that’s a very good success rate for the attacker. If I can try repeatedly, or choose which inputs to attack, I don’t need to win every time. I just need to find one failure that accomplishes my goal. So the question is less whether 70% sounds like high accuracy and more whether the failures that remain are enough for an attacker to exploit.

r001.rationale: The response says an attacker can try repeatedly and needs only one failure, but it does not communicate the specific idea that trying about four times makes at least one success probable.

sol-6.1.text: From the attacker’s perspective, 70% accuracy means I can cause a failure 30% of the time. And depending on what I’m trying to do, that might be more than enough. If I can try repeatedly, or choose which examples to attack, I don’t need to defeat the system on every input. I just need to find a failure that serves my purpose. So the important question is what the attacker gets to do and what counts as success. An average accuracy number by itself doesn’t tell you whether the system is secure.

r001.rationale: The response says 70% accuracy implies a 30% failure chance and mentions repeated attempts, but it does not state that about four tries will probably yield at least one success.
